Why Handwritten Thank You Notes Still Matter

I recently spent an afternoon walking around my family’s farm in upstate New York, looking for a little inspiration. I ended up at my grandfather’s sap house, where we made our own maple syrup. We gathered sap from the trees, brought it down in huge vats, and boiled it down to that delicious, sugary syrup, all right there on the farm. We’ve been in the maple syrup business for about 25 years.
While I was rummaging through the sap house, I found something I didn’t expect: a handwritten thank-you note.

Over the years, my grandfather was thanked hundreds, if not thousands, of times. Whenever a guest or family member visited, he’d send them home with a jug of syrup. He never kept track of any of it. But here was a note from a visitor he’d given a jug to. She’d taken the time to write and thank him for the gesture.
That note had probably been sitting there for 30 years. The paper was old, yellowed, and worn, and it was still there. That’s the raw power of a simple handwritten thank-you.

In my sales training sessions, we talk all the time about the power of a small, simple gesture. When you send a handwritten note to a prospect, a customer, or a coworker, it’s something they tend to hold on to. I had the proof in my hand.
When to Send a Handwritten Thank You Note
You may think you need a rare, special occasion to send a thank you note, but there are several moments where a note has the most impact:
After a first meeting with a prospect, to thank them for their time.
After a deal closes, to thank your new customer for their trust.
After a referral, to thank the person who put their name behind you.
When a customer goes out of their way, like making an introduction or giving you feedback.
With a gift, so it feels personal instead of corporate. (Here are client gift ideas that pair well with a note.)
When a teammate helps you, like the operations lead who rushed an order or the colleague who covered a call.
What to Write in a Business Thank You Note
A good thank-you note is short and sweet. Usually, just three or four sentences will do the job.
Start with the thank-you. Say exactly what you’re thanking them for.
Get specific. Mention a detail from your conversation or something they did that mattered.
Look ahead. Add one line about the relationship going forward, without asking for anything.
It may be tempting, but leave out the sales pitch, and definitely don’t tuck in a business card or brochure. The moment the note asks for something, it stops being a thank-you.
To a prospect after a first meeting:

Dear Sarah, thank you for taking the time to meet with me on Tuesday. I enjoyed hearing how your team is preparing for the new territory launch, and your plan for the first 90 days was impressive. I’m looking forward to our next conversation. — Mike
To a new customer after a deal closes:
Dear Tom, thank you for trusting us with your team’s training this year. I know it was a big decision, and I don’t take it lightly. I’m excited to see what your team accomplishes. — Jessica
To a client who sent a referral:
Dear Lisa, thank you for introducing me to Mark. It means a lot that you’d put your name behind us. I’ll take good care of him. — Chris
Dana, thank you for staying late to get the Henderson order out on time. You saved that account, and I won’t forget it. — Alex

Use a quality card instead of a sticky note or printer paper. Write legibly, and if your handwriting is rough, slow down and keep it short. Address the envelope by hand and use a real stamp, since a printed label makes it look like marketing mail.

Here’s the challenge I’ll leave you with: can you find five people to drop a handwritten note in the mail to every month? Set a monthly reminder on your calendar. Keep a box of cards and stamps at your desk so there’s nothing slowing you down, and mail each note within a day or two while the moment is still fresh.

Common Questions About Handwritten Thank You Notes
Are handwritten thank you notes still effective in business?
Yes. Because most communication is digital, a handwritten note stands out. People often keep them for years, which keeps you top of mind long after an email would be forgotten.
What should you write in a thank you note to a customer?

Thank them for something specific, mention a detail that shows you were paying attention, and add one line about looking forward to working together. Keep it to three or four sentences, and leave out any sales pitch.
Should you send handwritten notes to prospects?

Yes. A short handwritten note after a first meeting thanks the prospect for their time and helps you stand out from salespeople who only send emails. Keep it personal and avoid pitching. How soon should you send a thank you note?
Within a day or two. The sooner it arrives, the more connected it feels to the moment you’re thanking them for.
